metadata.purpose: Establish the universal evidence ontology, classification, lifecycle, quality, strength, reliability, and AI reasoning foundation for the Pipeline Assessment Engine.

evidenceOntology.definition: Evidence represents observable, verifiable, or customer-confirmed information that increases or decreases confidence that a pipeline can successfully achieve Closed Won.

evidenceCategories.purpose: Validate customer business problem, business impact, strategic importance, and urgency.
Validate customer stakeholders, roles, authority, influence, alignment, and executive sponsorship.
Validate the customer decision journey, decision criteria, approval governance, procurement process, and decision timeline.
Validate solution requirements, solution fit, differentiated value, technical feasibility, operational fit, and implementation feasibility.
Validate the competitive landscape, incumbent position, alternative solutions, customer preference, and differentiation.
Validate budget, funding, commercial model, pricing alignment, contractual conditions, and commercial feasibility.
Validate delivery capability, implementation readiness, internal resource readiness, customer readiness, and execution feasibility.
Validate engagement momentum, customer commitment, milestone progression, timeline adherence, and closing trajectory.

evidenceTypes.description: Objective information directly observed, measured, or documented.
Information explicitly confirmed by a customer stakeholder.
Evidence that validates a business assumption, solution requirement, value proposition, technical capability, or implementation assumption.
Evidence demonstrating an explicit customer commitment, action, approval, or next-step agreement.
Observable customer behavior that indicates buying intent, engagement, resistance, or momentum.
Evidence contained within formal customer, commercial, technical, procurement, or project documentation.
Evidence automatically generated from CRM, sales activity, communication, workflow, or other business systems.

evidenceSources.description: Direct conversation with an executive or senior decision-maker.
Structured customer discovery, solution validation, business case, technical, or planning workshop.
Information captured during customer meetings and interactions.
Customer-provided formal documents such as requirements, specifications, business cases, project plans, procurement documents, or approval documents.
System-recorded sales activity, stakeholder interaction, meeting, task, stage, or engagement information.
Seller-provided interpretation, judgment, assumption, or manually entered pipeline information.
Market, competitor, industry, public, partner, or third-party intelligence.

states.description: No meaningful evidence currently exists.
Potential evidence or information has been identified but has not yet been sufficiently validated.
Evidence has been captured from an available source.
Evidence has been reviewed and determined to be sufficiently reliable for assessment.
Evidence has been explicitly confirmed by an appropriate customer stakeholder or authoritative source.
Previously valid evidence has become outdated and requires revalidation.
Evidence has been determined to be unreliable, contradictory, invalid, or otherwise unsuitable for assessment.

evidenceQualityAttributes.definition: Whether the evidence contains concrete, specific, and decision-relevant information rather than generic statements or assumptions.
The credibility and authority of the source providing the evidence.
How recently the evidence was created, observed, or validated.
Whether the customer or another authoritative source explicitly validates the evidence.
Whether the evidence sufficiently covers the information required to support the associated assessment.
Whether the evidence is consistent with other available evidence, customer statements, system data, and observed behavior.

evidenceStrengthModel.purpose: Provide a universal qualitative and quantitative foundation for evaluating the confidence strength of individual evidence objects.

strengthLevels.description: Direct, recent, specific, reliable, and customer-confirmed evidence with strong decision relevance.
Relevant evidence exists but is partially indirect, incomplete, insufficiently confirmed, or subject to moderate uncertainty.
Indirect, assumption-based, outdated, incomplete, or weakly validated evidence.
No meaningful evidence exists or available information is insufficient to establish confidence.

evidenceReliabilityRules.rule: Customer-confirmed evidence should receive higher confidence than seller assumptions or interpretations when evaluating the same proposition.
Recent evidence should generally receive higher confidence than materially outdated evidence, subject to the nature and expected validity period of the evidence.
Multiple independent and consistent evidence sources should increase confidence in the underlying proposition.
Missing evidence should normally increase uncertainty and reduce confidence but should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the pipeline will be lost.
The quality and strength of evidence should determine how strongly the evidence influences the associated assessment dimension and win probability.
Materially contradictory evidence should reduce confidence and trigger additional validation rather than allowing the stronger-looking evidence to be accepted without investigation.
Evidence must be interpreted within the applicable revenue motion, industry, customer context, pipeline stage, and buying situation.
Evidence should remain valid only for an appropriate period based on its nature; time-sensitive evidence should be revalidated when material pipeline conditions change.

reasoningPrinciples: Absence of evidence represents uncertainty rather than automatic failure.
Customer-confirmed evidence receives the highest priority when evaluating customer-specific propositions.
Evidence must be interpreted within the applicable industry and revenue motion context.
Evidence quality, reliability, freshness, completeness, consistency, and customer validation should influence confidence.
Contradictory evidence should trigger investigation and revalidation rather than being ignored.
Evidence should be evaluated in relation to the specific PADF dimension it supports.
Evidence should contribute to an evolving assessment rather than being treated as permanently static.
Changes in evidence should be capable of changing risk assessment and win probability over time.
reasoningQuestions: What specific proposition does this evidence support?
Who provided or generated this evidence?
How reliable is the evidence source?
When was this evidence created or last validated?
Has the customer explicitly confirmed the evidence?
Is the evidence specific and measurable enough to support a decision?
Is the evidence complete enough to support the associated assessment?
Is the evidence consistent with other available information?
How does this evidence affect the associated PADF dimension?
How does this evidence affect current win probability?
What additional evidence is required to increase confidence?

metadata.purpose: Define the universal mapping between the eight Pipeline Assessment Dimensions and the evidence categories, evidence roles, evidence requirements, and evidence coverage principles used by the Pipeline Assessment Engine.
metadata.designPrinciple: Every PADF assessment should be grounded in relevant, traceable, and contextually appropriate evidence.

padfEvidenceMappingPrinciples.description: Every PADF dimension must be assessed through evidence that directly relates to the business proposition represented by that dimension.
Each PADF dimension should have a defined set of primary evidence categories that provide the strongest basis for assessment.
Secondary evidence may strengthen, validate, or contextualize primary evidence but should not automatically substitute for critical primary evidence.
Material pipeline judgments should preferably be supported by multiple relevant evidence types or independent evidence sources.
Evidence directly confirmed or demonstrated by the customer should generally carry greater assessment relevance than seller assumptions.
Evidence relevance and interpretation may vary by revenue motion, industry, customer context, and pipeline stage.
The absence of expected evidence must remain visible as an evidence gap and contribute to assessment uncertainty.
Evidence mappings must support the historical evolution of evidence as a pipeline progresses toward Closed Won or Closed Lost.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the customer has a sufficiently important, quantified, urgent, and strategically relevant reason to purchase.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence that the customer has a clearly defined business problem, operational challenge, strategic initiative, or measurable opportunity.
Evidence quantifying the financial, operational, strategic, regulatory, risk, productivity, revenue, or other material impact of the customer problem.
Evidence demonstrating why the customer needs to act within a meaningful timeframe.
Evidence that the initiative is connected to an organizational strategy, transformation program, executive priority, or important business objective.
Evidence demonstrating the consequences of delaying, rejecting, or maintaining the current state.
Customer-confirmed evidence that the proposed business outcome is meaningful and worth pursuing.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the sales team has sufficient access, influence, alignment, and sponsorship across the customer buying center.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence identifying and validating the person or role with authority over the relevant investment decision.
Evidence that an influential executive actively supports the initiative.
Evidence that an internal customer champion actively advocates for the solution and helps advance the buying process.
Evidence that the relevant decision-makers, influencers, users, technical stakeholders, procurement stakeholders, and blockers have been identified.
Evidence that relevant customer stakeholders are aligned around the problem, solution, value, and decision.
Evidence demonstrating meaningful access to influential customer stakeholders.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine how well the sales team understands and can influence the customer's decision process, decision criteria, governance, procurement, and timeline.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence that the customer decision process and major decision steps are understood.
Evidence identifying the customer's formal and informal criteria for selecting a solution or supplier.
Evidence identifying the required internal approvals, governance checkpoints, and authorization mechanisms.
Evidence that procurement, tendering, contracting, vendor qualification, or purchasing processes are understood.
Evidence supporting the expected decision date and the milestones required to reach it.
Evidence that buyer and seller have aligned on actions, responsibilities, milestones, and target dates.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the proposed solution is demonstrably aligned with customer requirements and provides sufficient differentiated value to justify selection.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence that the proposed solution satisfies identified customer business, functional, technical, operational, or project requirements.
Evidence that relevant technical, architectural, operational, engineering, or performance assumptions have been validated.
Evidence demonstrating the measurable value the proposed solution creates for the customer.
Evidence demonstrating why the proposed solution is materially preferable to alternatives.
Evidence generated through demonstrations, proof of concept, pilot, reference project, test, benchmark, prototype, or other validation mechanism.
Explicit customer confirmation that the proposed solution addresses the relevant requirements and expected outcomes.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine the strength of the seller's position against named competitors, incumbent suppliers, internal alternatives, substitute solutions, and the status quo.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence identifying relevant competitors, incumbents, alternatives, and the status quo.
Evidence describing how the customer evaluates competing solutions or suppliers.
Evidence proving meaningful differentiation against competing alternatives.
Evidence indicating customer preference for the seller's solution.
Evidence demonstrating the customer's willingness and ability to replace an incumbent or existing solution.
Evidence revealing competitor strengths, customer objections, incumbent advantages, or threats to the seller's position.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the financial, pricing, contracting, funding, procurement, and commercial conditions support a viable path to Closed Won.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence that sufficient customer funding or budget exists or can realistically be secured.
Evidence validating the commercial model, pricing structure, purchasing mechanism, and expected transaction structure.
Evidence regarding procurement requirements, commercial evaluation, vendor qualification, and purchasing conditions.
Evidence that contractual requirements, legal conditions, terms, and approval processes are understood and manageable.
Evidence that the customer considers the proposed commercial structure acceptable.
Evidence that funding availability and timing align with the expected closing schedule.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the seller and customer have sufficient capability, resources, planning, delivery confidence, and execution readiness to successfully move the pipeline to Closed Won and fulfill the resulting commitment.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence that the seller can deliver the proposed solution, service, project, or contractual commitment.
Evidence that required internal and customer resources are available or can be mobilized.
Evidence that a credible implementation, delivery, deployment, or project execution plan exists.
Evidence that the customer is prepared to provide required resources, access, decisions, data, infrastructure, or organizational support.
Evidence identifying delivery, implementation, resource, technical, operational, contractual, or organizational execution risks.
Evidence from relevant prior projects, customer references, delivery track record, certifications, or demonstrated capability.

padfEvidenceMappings.dimensionPurpose: Determine whether the pipeline is progressing with sufficient customer engagement, commitment, milestone achievement, decision velocity, and near-term closeability.

criticalEvidenceRoles.description: Evidence showing sustained and meaningful customer engagement.
Evidence that the customer is taking concrete actions that advance the buying process.
Evidence that agreed pipeline milestones are being completed on schedule.
Evidence that customer decisions and required approvals are progressing at an appropriate pace.
Evidence supporting the credibility of the expected close date.
Evidence of declining engagement, delayed milestones, unresolved blockers, stakeholder withdrawal, or other indicators of pipeline deterioration.

crossDimensionEvidenceMappings.description: Evidence demonstrating customer business value primarily supports Customer Value & Urgency and may also validate Solution Value Proposition and Momentum & Closeability.
Executive sponsorship primarily validates buying-center influence but can also strengthen strategic urgency and closeability.
Decision criteria primarily support Buying Process Control while also influencing solution fit and competitive position.
Solution validation primarily supports Solution Value Proposition and may also strengthen customer value, competitive position, and execution readiness.
Customer preference primarily validates Competitive Position and may also support solution differentiation and closeability.
Budget approval primarily supports Commercial Deal Structure but also provides evidence of stakeholder authority, decision-process progression, and closeability.
Implementation readiness primarily supports Sales Execution Readiness while also validating solution feasibility and pipeline progression.
Customer commitment primarily supports Momentum & Closeability and may provide evidence of stakeholder alignment, decision-process progression, and commercial readiness.

coverageLevels.definition: Minimum evidence required to establish a meaningful assessment baseline for the PADF dimension.
Evidence expected for a reasonably confident assessment of the PADF dimension.
Additional evidence that materially increases confidence and reduces uncertainty.

coverageInterpretationRules.rule: A dimension should not be treated as strongly supported solely because one evidence item exists.
Critical evidence gaps should remain visible even when supporting evidence is strong.
Evidence coverage must be evaluated together with evidence quality and strength.
The minimum evidence set establishes assessment eligibility but does not automatically imply a high dimension score.
Preferred and strong evidence increases assessment confidence but must remain relevant to the specific customer and pipeline.

flow: Pass evidence-supported assessment to Pipeline Qualification Rules

reasoningPrinciples: Start assessment from the PADF dimension and determine what evidence is expected for that dimension.
Prioritize primary evidence over secondary evidence.
Distinguish evidence existence from evidence strength.
Do not treat seller assumptions as equivalent to customer-confirmed evidence.
Use cross-dimension evidence carefully because one evidence item may support multiple dimensions without fully satisfying all of them.
Identify material evidence gaps before increasing confidence in a dimension.
Interpret evidence according to the applicable revenue motion and industry context when those layers become available.
Preserve evidence provenance and historical timing when assessing pipeline evolution.
diagnosticQuestions: What PADF dimension is being assessed?
What evidence should exist for this dimension?
Which evidence category provides the primary basis for assessment?
Which critical evidence roles have been satisfied?
How strong is the available evidence?
Is the evidence customer-confirmed or seller-assumed?
Is the evidence current and contextually relevant?
How does the evidence change confidence in this dimension?

metadata.purpose: Define the reusable universal evidence objects used by the Pipeline Assessment Engine to collect, interpret, validate, and reason about pipeline evidence.
metadata.designPrinciple: Reusable evidence objects with universal business meaning, explicit PADF relationships, evidence-source guidance, strength indicators, validation questions, and risk relevance.

evidenceObjectDesignPrinciples.description: Each evidence object must be reusable across supported revenue motions and industries unless explicitly overridden by later configuration layers.
Each evidence object should represent a distinct proposition that can be independently evaluated.
Each evidence object must map to one primary PADF dimension and may map to additional secondary dimensions where appropriate.
Evidence definitions should describe observable, verifiable, or customer-confirmable information rather than abstract seller opinions.
Each evidence object must distinguish strong evidence from moderate, weak, assumed, or missing evidence.
Evidence gaps should be interpretable as actionable information that can support risk detection and winning strategy recommendations.
Evidence must be capable of becoming outdated and therefore support validation and revalidation over the pipeline lifecycle.
Evidence directly confirmed or demonstrated by the customer should generally carry greater confidence than seller assumptions.

evidenceObjects.definition: A clearly articulated customer business problem, operational challenge, strategic issue, or opportunity that the proposed solution is intended to address.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes that the pipeline is associated with a real customer business need rather than a seller-generated opportunity.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A clearly defined business problem is the foundation for validating value, urgency, solution relevance, and customer motivation.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Problem is specific to the customer's business.
Problem is recognized by relevant customer stakeholders.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Problem is based primarily on seller assumptions.
Problem is described in generic industry terms.
No customer stakeholder has confirmed the problem.
validationQuestions: What specific business problem is the customer trying to solve?
Who within the customer organization recognizes this problem?
What happens if the problem is not addressed?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the business, financial, operational, strategic, risk, productivity, revenue, or other material impact of the customer problem has been quantified or credibly estimated.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates the economic significance of solving the problem.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Quantified impact provides the foundation for business-case justification and executive-level buying motivation.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Financial or operational impact is quantified.
Impact is linked to recognized business KPIs.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Impact is expressed only qualitatively.
Seller estimates impact without customer validation.
No baseline exists.
validationQuestions: What measurable business impact does the problem create?
What is the current baseline?
How was the impact estimate calculated?
Has the customer validated the estimate?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer considers the issue sufficiently important to require action within a defined or meaningful timeframe.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes whether the pipeline has genuine customer-driven urgency.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Without urgency, a pipeline may remain indefinitely open even when the customer recognizes the problem.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer explicitly identifies a deadline or required action date.
Urgency is linked to a business event or consequence.
Customer has committed resources or actions to address the issue.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Urgency is based only on the seller's target close date.
Customer expresses general interest without action.
No consequence exists for delay.
validationQuestions: Why does the customer need to act now?
What happens if the decision is delayed?
Is there a customer-driven deadline?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer initiative is connected to a recognized organizational strategy, executive priority, transformation program, or important business objective.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates that the pipeline is strategically relevant to the customer organization.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Strategic alignment increases organizational attention, sponsorship, and resource availability.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Initiative appears in an approved strategy or program.
Executive stakeholder explicitly links the initiative to a strategic priority.
Resources have been allocated to the initiative.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Strategic relevance is inferred by the seller.
No executive or organizational confirmation exists.
validationQuestions: Which strategic priority does this initiative support?
Who owns that strategic priority?
How important is this initiative relative to competing priorities?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating the material consequences of delaying, rejecting, or maintaining the current state.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes the economic or strategic pressure created by inaction.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A compelling cost of inaction can create decision urgency and reduce the attractiveness of waiting.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Consequences are hypothetical.
No measurable impact of delay exists.
validationQuestions: What happens if the customer does nothing?
What is the cost of delaying the initiative?
Which business objectives are affected by inaction?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer explicitly recognizes the proposed business outcomes as meaningful and valuable.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Confirms that seller-defined value is aligned with customer-perceived value.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Customer validation prevents the sales team from building a business case around internally assumed value.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer links value to measurable KPIs.
Value is accepted by relevant stakeholders.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Value proposition is seller-generated.
Customer acknowledges capability but not business value.
validationQuestions: Which outcomes does the customer consider most valuable?
How will the customer measure success?
Has the customer agreed with the proposed value?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the relevant customer stakeholders, roles, influencers, users, decision-makers, procurement participants, and potential blockers have been identified.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides visibility into the customer political and decision environment.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unknown stakeholders create hidden influence and decision risks.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Relevant stakeholder roles are explicitly identified.
Influence and decision responsibilities are understood.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Only one customer contact is known.
Stakeholder roles are assumed.
Economic buyer or procurement participants are unknown.
validationQuestions: Who is involved in the decision?
Who influences the decision?
Who can block the decision?
Who will use or operate the solution?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence identifying the person or organizational role with authority over the relevant investment decision.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes whether the sales team understands who controls the economic decision.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A pipeline without access to economic decision authority carries significant closing uncertainty.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Authority has been confirmed through customer interaction.
Economic buyer's decision criteria are understood.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Economic buyer is inferred from title alone.
Seller has never validated authority.
validationQuestions: Who ultimately approves the investment?
Who controls the relevant budget?
What does that person need to see before approving?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that an influential customer executive actively supports the initiative and is willing to help advance it.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates executive-level sponsorship.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Executive sponsorship can accelerate decisions, resolve internal conflicts, and protect strategic initiatives.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Executive has explicitly endorsed the initiative.
Executive participates in important decision activities.
Executive provides resources or removes blockers.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Executive name is known but engagement is absent.
Seller assumes executive support based on organizational hierarchy.
validationQuestions: Who is the executive sponsor?
What action has the executive taken to support the initiative?
When did the executive last engage?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that an internal customer stakeholder actively advocates for the seller's solution and helps navigate the buying process.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates internal customer advocacy.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A genuine champion can provide intelligence, influence stakeholders, and advance internal activities when the seller is not present.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Champion helps obtain stakeholder access or advance milestones.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Contact is friendly but takes no advocacy action.
Seller labels a contact as champion without behavioral evidence.
validationQuestions: What has the stakeholder done internally to advance the opportunity?
Can the stakeholder influence other decision-makers?
What information does the stakeholder provide that the seller could not obtain independently?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that relevant customer stakeholders share sufficient alignment around the problem, desired outcome, solution direction, and decision.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Shows that the pipeline has organizational rather than individual-level support.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Misalignment among stakeholders can create late-stage objections or decision delays.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Multiple stakeholder groups agree on major requirements and outcomes.
Key stakeholders participate in aligned planning.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Only one stakeholder supports the initiative.
Stakeholder priorities remain contradictory.
validationQuestions: Do business, technical, procurement, and executive stakeholders agree?
Where do stakeholder priorities differ?
What unresolved stakeholder conflict remains?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the sales team has meaningful and continuing access to influential customer stakeholders.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Measures the practical ability to influence the buying center.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Knowing stakeholders without being able to engage them limits sales control.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Seller has recurring access to key stakeholders.
Stakeholders proactively engage with the seller.
Access includes decision-makers rather than only users or intermediaries.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Access is limited to a single operational contact.
Meetings with decision-makers repeatedly fail to occur.
validationQuestions: Which influential stakeholders can the seller directly engage?
How frequently are key stakeholders engaged?
Which important stakeholders remain inaccessible?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the major stages, participants, governance checkpoints, and actions required for the customer to make a decision are understood.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes visibility into how the customer will actually make the purchase decision.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unknown decision processes create hidden delays and false close-date assumptions.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Approval and evaluation stages are documented.
Required stakeholders and milestones are identified.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller relies on generic assumptions about the customer's process.
Decision stages are unknown.
validationQuestions: What steps must the customer complete before making the decision?
Who owns each step?
What approvals are required?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence identifying the customer's formal and informal criteria for evaluating and selecting a solution or supplier.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Shows what factors will determine the buying decision.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Winning requires alignment with the criteria that actually drive selection.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Relative importance of criteria is understood.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Criteria are inferred from an RFP alone.
Seller assumes price or technical capability is the main criterion.
validationQuestions: What are the customer's selection criteria?
Which criteria matter most?
Who defines and scores the criteria?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence identifying the internal governance, approval authorities, committees, or formal checkpoints required before the purchase can proceed.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Reveals the organizational authorization path.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Late discovery of approval requirements is a common cause of pipeline slippage.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Required documentation or thresholds are known.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Approval path is unknown.
Seller assumes the contacted stakeholder can approve.
validationQuestions: Who must approve the purchase?
What governance bodies are involved?
What documentation is required for approval?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that procurement, tendering, vendor qualification, contracting, purchasing, or sourcing requirements are understood.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes whether the commercial buying mechanism is known and manageable.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Procurement requirements can materially alter the competitive and timing dynamics of a pipeline.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Procurement involvement is unknown.
Seller assumes informal purchasing.
validationQuestions: What procurement process must the customer follow?
Is a tender or formal sourcing process required?
What vendor qualification steps remain?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence supporting a customer-driven decision timeline with identifiable milestones and target dates.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Tests whether the expected decision date is grounded in customer reality.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A seller-created close date is not sufficient evidence of closeability.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Milestones leading to the decision are identified.
Dates are tied to customer business events or governance.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Close date exists only in CRM.
Customer has not committed to a decision timeframe.
validationQuestions: When does the customer intend to make the decision?
What milestones must occur first?
What customer event drives the date?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that buyer and seller have mutually agreed on actions, responsibilities, milestones, dependencies, and target dates required to progress the pipeline.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates shared commitment to the buying journey.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Mutual planning increases transparency and reduces ambiguity around next steps.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Both parties agree to the plan.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Plan is created only by the seller.
Customer has not accepted responsibilities.
validationQuestions: Has the customer agreed to the action plan?
Which customer actions are scheduled?
Which dependencies could delay the plan?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the proposed solution satisfies the customer's identified business, functional, technical, operational, or project requirements.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes fundamental solution fit.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A pipeline cannot be won if the proposed solution fails critical customer requirements.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Fit is assumed from product capability.
Critical requirements remain unclear.
validationQuestions: What are the customer's critical requirements?
Which requirements are fully satisfied?
Which requirements remain unresolved?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that relevant technical, architectural, operational, engineering, performance, integration, or feasibility assumptions have been validated.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Reduces uncertainty around whether the solution can technically satisfy the customer's environment.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unvalidated technical assumptions can create late-stage objections and execution risk.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Relevant tests or assessments are completed.
Critical integration or performance assumptions are confirmed.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Technical feasibility is assumed.
Important technical dependencies remain untested.
validationQuestions: Which technical assumptions have been validated?
What technical risks remain?
Who on the customer side has approved the technical fit?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer recognizes the proposed solution's capabilities and outcomes as relevant to its defined business needs.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Connects solution capability with customer-perceived value.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Feature acceptance without value acceptance does not necessarily create buying preference.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer articulates the value of the proposed solution.
Value is linked to business outcomes.
Value is recognized by decision-relevant stakeholders.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller describes value without customer confirmation.
Customer shows technical interest but no business-value recognition.
validationQuestions: What does the customer believe the solution will achieve?
Which capabilities create the most value?
Has the customer explicitly validated the value proposition?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating that the seller's solution provides materially differentiated value relative to relevant alternatives.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Creates a reason for the customer to prefer the seller's solution.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Solution fit alone may not produce a win when multiple alternatives can satisfy the requirements.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Differentiators map directly to customer priorities.
Differentiation is difficult for competitors to replicate.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Differentiation consists of generic marketing claims.
Customer does not recognize the differentiation.
validationQuestions: Why would the customer choose this solution over alternatives?
Which differentiators matter to the customer?
Has the customer explicitly recognized those differentiators?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence generated through a demonstration, proof of concept, pilot, test, benchmark, prototype, reference project, or other structured validation mechanism.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides direct evidence that the solution can deliver expected outcomes.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Proof reduces uncertainty where customer risk perception is high.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Validation activity addresses critical customer requirements.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Demonstration is generic.
No customer acceptance criteria exist.
validationQuestions: What was tested?
What were the agreed acceptance criteria?
Did the customer confirm the results?

evidenceObjects.definition: Explicit customer confirmation that the proposed solution satisfies the relevant requirements and expected outcomes.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Represents direct customer validation of solution acceptability.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Customer confirmation is materially stronger than seller interpretation of solution fit.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Decision-relevant customer stakeholder explicitly confirms solution acceptance.
Solution is accepted for the next buying step.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Only operational users express satisfaction.
Customer remains undecided about solution fit.
validationQuestions: Has the customer explicitly confirmed that the solution meets its needs?
Who has provided the confirmation?
What objections remain?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence identifying named competitors, incumbents, internal alternatives, substitute solutions, and the status quo relevant to the customer's decision.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes the actual competitive environment.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unknown competition creates blind spots in strategy and forecasting.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Status quo is treated as a competitive alternative.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller assumes no competition.
Competitive assessment is based only on market knowledge.
validationQuestions: Who else is being considered?
What happens if the customer does nothing?
Is there an incumbent supplier?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the seller understands how the customer compares competing solutions or suppliers.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Reveals the basis on which competitive preference will be established.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Competitive strategy must address the criteria the customer actually uses.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Criteria are confirmed with decision-relevant stakeholders.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller assumes evaluation criteria.
Only generic market comparisons exist.
validationQuestions: How will the customer compare suppliers?
Which capabilities differentiate the alternatives?
What factors could cause the customer to select a competitor?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating that the seller has a meaningful and customer-relevant advantage over competing alternatives.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes a credible competitive reason to win.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A seller needs a defensible reason to be selected when alternatives satisfy the basic requirements.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Differentiation is tied to customer priorities.
Competitive weakness of alternatives is understood.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Differentiation is generic.
Seller cannot identify why it should win.
validationQuestions: What is the seller's strongest competitive advantage?
Why does that advantage matter to this customer?
Has the customer acknowledged the advantage?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence indicating that the customer currently prefers the seller's solution or intends to select the seller over relevant alternatives.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Represents actual customer preference rather than seller optimism.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Preference is one of the strongest indicators of competitive win potential before formal award.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer requests seller-specific commercial or contractual steps.
Customer gives seller privileged access or information.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller interprets engagement as preference.
Customer states that all suppliers remain equally positioned.
validationQuestions: Where does the seller currently stand against alternatives?
What evidence indicates customer preference?
What could still change that preference?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating that the customer has both motivation and practical ability to replace an incumbent or existing solution.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Measures the feasibility of displacing the current provider or status quo.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Incumbents often possess structural advantages that cannot be overcome through product superiority alone.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer has identified dissatisfaction with incumbent.
Customer has a defined reason for switching.
Switching requirements and barriers are understood.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Incumbent dissatisfaction is assumed.
Switching barriers remain unknown.
validationQuestions: Why would the customer change from the incumbent?
What prevents the customer from changing?
What event could trigger replacement?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence identifying competitor strengths, customer objections, incumbent advantages, or other factors that could materially reduce the seller's probability of winning.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides visibility into threats against the current position.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Winning strategy requires understanding not only why the seller can win but also why it could lose.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Seller claims competitors are weak without evidence.
Competitive threats are not actively monitored.
validationQuestions: What is the strongest competitor?
Where is the competitor stronger?
What could cause the customer to choose the competitor?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that sufficient customer funding or budget exists or can realistically be secured for the purchase.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes whether the customer can financially execute the purchase.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Strong customer interest without funding does not create a viable commercial pipeline.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Budget timing aligns with the purchase.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Budget is assumed.
Customer says budget may be available without confirmation.
validationQuestions: Is budget already allocated?
Who controls the budget?
When will funding become available?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence validating the expected pricing model, transaction structure, purchasing mechanism, commercial scope, and financial structure.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes the commercial shape of the transaction.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unclear commercial structure creates uncertainty around both deal viability and closing timing.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer understands and accepts the commercial model.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Commercial structure remains conceptual.
Customer has not validated purchasing assumptions.
validationQuestions: How will the customer purchase the solution?
What commercial structure does the customer expect?
Which commercial assumptions remain unresolved?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that procurement-specific commercial requirements, vendor conditions, pricing procedures, tender requirements, or sourcing rules are understood.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Shows that the seller can navigate the customer's commercial buying mechanism.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Commercial procurement requirements can materially affect pricing, eligibility, competition, and timing.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Procurement conditions are unknown.
Seller relies on assumptions about purchasing.
validationQuestions: What commercial procurement requirements must be satisfied?
How will pricing be evaluated?
What vendor conditions remain unresolved?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that contractual requirements, legal conditions, terms, liabilities, approvals, and negotiation requirements are understood.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes visibility into contractual closing risk.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Contracting issues discovered late can delay or prevent an otherwise successful commercial decision.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Material legal or contractual issues are identified.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Legal requirements are unknown.
Seller assumes standard terms will be accepted.
validationQuestions: What contractual requirements must be satisfied?
Which terms are likely to require negotiation?
Who approves the contract?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer considers the proposed commercial structure, pricing direction, and transaction conditions acceptable enough to proceed.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Indicates that commercial resistance has been sufficiently reduced.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A technically preferred solution can still lose because the commercial proposition is unacceptable.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer progresses to final commercial steps.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Customer has not reviewed commercial terms.
Commercial acceptance is inferred from continued engagement.
validationQuestions: Has the customer accepted the commercial direction?
What commercial objections remain?
What needs to happen before commercial agreement?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that customer funding availability and budget timing align with the expected decision and closing schedule.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Tests whether funding timing supports the forecasted close.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Budget may exist but still be unavailable during the expected closing period.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Funding timing matches customer decision timeline.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Funding timing is uncertain.
Budget exists but release depends on unknown events.
validationQuestions: When will funding become available?
What event releases the budget?
Does funding timing support the expected close date?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the seller has the technical, operational, organizational, and delivery capability required to fulfill the proposed customer commitment.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Establishes execution credibility.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Customer confidence can be undermined when delivery capability is uncertain.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Required resources and expertise are available.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Capability depends on unconfirmed future resources.
Seller has limited relevant delivery experience.
validationQuestions: What capabilities are required to deliver?
Does the seller have those capabilities today?
What capability gaps remain?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that required internal seller resources and customer-side resources are available or committed.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Tests whether the people, expertise, capacity, and organizational resources required for execution can be mobilized.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Resource gaps can create delivery delays and reduce customer confidence.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Resources are planned but not confirmed.
Critical roles remain unfilled.
validationQuestions: Which resources are required?
Who has committed those resources?
Are there capacity constraints?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that a credible implementation, deployment, delivery, engineering, project, or service execution plan exists.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides a concrete view of how the customer commitment would be executed.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A credible delivery plan reduces perceived execution risk.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Plan includes milestones, responsibilities, dependencies, and timing.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Plan is generic.
Customer has not reviewed the plan.
validationQuestions: What are the major delivery milestones?
What customer dependencies exist?
Has the customer accepted the execution approach?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer is prepared to provide required resources, access, data, infrastructure, decisions, approvals, and organizational support for execution.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Tests customer-side readiness.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Seller readiness alone cannot guarantee successful implementation.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Required access or data is available.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Customer responsibilities remain undefined.
Required customer resources are unavailable.
validationQuestions: What must the customer provide?
Who owns those responsibilities?
Are customer dependencies ready?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that material delivery, implementation, technical, operational, resource, organizational, or contractual execution risks have been identified and have credible mitigation plans.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates execution risk awareness and control.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Unmanaged execution risks can undermine both winning confidence and post-sale performance.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Owners and mitigation actions are assigned.
Customer and seller agree on critical mitigations.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Risks are not formally assessed.
Mitigation depends on future assumptions.
validationQuestions: What could prevent successful execution?
Who owns each major risk?
What mitigation actions are already underway?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating relevant prior delivery experience, customer references, certifications, successful implementations, or demonstrated capability.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides external credibility for execution capability.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Relevant references reduce perceived implementation and supplier risk.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Reference is materially similar to the customer's situation.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Reference is unrelated to the customer's context.
Seller cites generic logos without relevant proof.
validationQuestions: Which prior customer example is most relevant?
What measurable outcome did the reference achieve?
Can the prospect validate the reference?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence showing sustained, meaningful, and progressively deeper customer engagement over time.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Measures whether customer activity is moving the pipeline forward.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: High engagement momentum is generally more predictive of progression than historical activity volume alone.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer proactively schedules or initiates interactions.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Activity is mostly seller initiated.
Meetings occur without meaningful progression.
validationQuestions: Who is initiating recent engagement?
Is engagement becoming deeper or more senior?
What customer actions demonstrate momentum?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that the customer is taking concrete actions that advance the buying process.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Demonstrates behavioral commitment rather than verbal interest.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Customer action is a stronger signal of buying intent than seller-reported interest.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer provides required information or approvals.
Customer schedules the next decision milestone.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Customer expresses interest but takes no action.
Actions are repeatedly postponed.
validationQuestions: What concrete action has the customer taken?
What has the customer committed to doing next?
Has the customer fulfilled previous commitments?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that agreed pipeline milestones are being completed according to plan.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Measures actual progress toward the customer decision.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Milestone completion provides objective evidence that the pipeline is advancing.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Each milestone unlocks a subsequent decision step.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Milestones exist only in CRM.
Repeated milestone slippage occurs.
validationQuestions: Which milestones have been completed?
Which milestones are delayed?
Who owns the next milestone?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence that customer decisions, approvals, evaluations, and required actions are progressing at an appropriate pace.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Measures the speed at which the customer moves through its decision process.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Slow decision velocity is a leading indicator of forecast and close-date risk.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Customer completes decisions within expected timeframes.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Decisions are repeatedly deferred.
Customer takes substantially longer than expected to act.
validationQuestions: How quickly is the customer making decisions?
Which decisions are delayed?
Why are decisions slowing down?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence demonstrating that the expected close date is supported by customer commitments, decision milestones, funding timing, and remaining actions.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Tests whether the forecasted close date is realistic.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: A pipeline may be healthy but still not close within the forecast period.
strongEvidenceIndicators: Required milestones fit within the timeline.
Funding and approval timing support the date.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Date is seller-generated.
Critical prerequisites remain unresolved.
validationQuestions: What evidence supports the expected close date?
Which prerequisites remain?
What customer event determines the closing date?

evidenceObjects.definition: Evidence indicating declining engagement, delayed milestones, stakeholder withdrawal, unresolved blockers, repeated rescheduling, or other deterioration in pipeline progression.
evidenceObjects.businessMeaning: Provides an early warning that pipeline momentum is weakening.
evidenceObjects.whyItMatters: Momentum deterioration often appears before a pipeline is formally moved to a later close date or Closed Lost.
weakEvidenceIndicators: Single isolated delay with a credible explanation.
Temporary scheduling issue without broader deterioration.
validationQuestions: What changed in customer behavior?
Which milestones have slipped?
Has stakeholder engagement declined?
What is causing the stall?

universalEvidenceInterpretationRules.rule: An evidence object represents a proposition to be evaluated, not a conclusion that the proposition is true.
Evidence should be evaluated according to its source, specificity, freshness, customer validation, completeness, and consistency.
Seller input can initiate an evidence record but should not automatically receive the same confidence as customer-confirmed evidence.
Evidence supporting multiple PADF dimensions should not automatically be counted as full evidence for every dimension.
Critical evidence gaps should remain visible even when other evidence in the same dimension is strong.
Contradictory evidence should trigger additional validation rather than being silently averaged away.
Evidence strength should be determined from evidence quality rather than from the evidence object's existence alone.
Evidence may become obsolete as the customer situation, decision process, competitive environment, funding, or stakeholder landscape changes.
The same evidence object may have different importance, interpretation, and expected strength across revenue motions and industries; such adaptations belong to later configuration layers.
Historical evidence states must be preserved so that the Pipeline Assessment Engine can explain how confidence, risk, and win probability evolved over time.

rules.name: Critical Evidence Dominance

rules.name: CustomerValidatedEvidencePreference
rules.description: Evidence directly validated by the customer should be interpreted as stronger than seller assumptions or internally inferred evidence.

rules.name: OutcomeEvidencePreference

rules.name: DecisionProcessEvidencePriority
rules.description: As a pipeline approaches late stages, evidence related to decision process, procurement, contracting, and award mechanics becomes increasingly important.

rules.name: RiskEvidenceEscalation
rules.description: Material negative evidence should increase risk severity rather than being neutralized by unrelated positive evidence.

rules.name: EvidenceRecency
rules.description: Recent evidence should generally carry greater predictive value than stale evidence unless the evidence represents a durable structural fact.

rules.name: EvidenceConsistency
rules.description: Consistent evidence across multiple stakeholders and sources increases confidence, while contradictory evidence should reduce confidence and trigger investigation.
rules.logic: multi_source_consistency increases confidence; contradiction decreases confidence

rules.name: MissingCriticalEvidence
rules.description: Missing critical evidence should be treated as an uncertainty or risk condition rather than automatically interpreted as negative evidence.

rules.name: EvidenceDependency
rules.description: Some evidence becomes meaningful only when prerequisite evidence exists.

rules.name: EvidenceEvolution
rules.description: Historical evidence should be retained so the engine can evaluate whether pipeline strength is improving, stagnating, or deteriorating over time.

scoringBands.description: Generic, vague, unsupported, or largely assumption-based evidence.
Some relevant information exists but lacks sufficient specificity or validation.
Relevant and reasonably specific evidence exists but important gaps remain.
Specific, relevant, and actionable evidence with limited uncertainty.
Highly specific, customer-relevant, well-documented, and decision-useful evidence.

evaluationDimensions.description: Evaluates the reliability and authority of the source from which the evidence originated.

sourceReliabilityLevels.description: Evidence explicitly confirmed by an authorized customer stakeholder.
Evidence provided directly by the economic decision-maker or equivalent authority.
Evidence provided by a senior customer sponsor with relevant authority.
Evidence provided by a stakeholder with direct decision authority.
Evidence provided by a technical authority responsible for validation.
Evidence provided by the accountable business owner.
Evidence provided by a supportive internal customer stakeholder.
Evidence provided by an operational user or influencer.
Evidence received from an external partner or intermediary.
Evidence derived from public sources or market information.
Evidence inferred by the seller without direct customer validation.
Evidence based primarily on unvalidated assumptions.

evaluationDimensions.description: Evaluates whether evidence has been confirmed, challenged, or independently validated.

states.description: Evidence has not been validated by a relevant stakeholder.

Evidence has been explicitly confirmed by a relevant customer stakeholder.

evaluationDimensions.description: Evaluates whether evidence remains current relative to the pipeline stage, sales cycle, and expected close date.

earlyStage.description: Evidence may remain useful for longer during early pipeline development.

lateStage.description: Late-stage evidence requires more frequent reconfirmation.

closingStage.description: Critical decision, commercial, and timing evidence should be highly current.

evaluationDimensions.description: Evaluates whether all expected attributes and validation elements for an evidence object have been sufficiently captured.

states.description: Material contradiction exists between evidence sources.
Important inconsistencies exist and materially reduce confidence.
Minor inconsistencies exist but the overall interpretation remains credible.
Evidence is generally consistent across relevant sources.

evidenceConfidenceModel.purpose: Calculate the confidence level associated with an evidence object before the evidence contributes to PADF dimension assessment.

confidenceBands.interpretation: Evidence should not materially influence assessment without further validation.
Evidence may indicate a hypothesis but should be treated as uncertain.
Evidence can contribute to assessment but requires caution and additional validation.
Evidence is sufficiently reliable for meaningful assessment contribution.
Evidence is highly reliable and can strongly support assessment conclusions.

confidenceCaps.reason: Seller inference or assumptions cannot create high confidence without validation.
Materially contradictory evidence requires resolution before confidence can increase.
Very stale evidence should not produce very high confidence.

evidenceStrengthModel.purpose: Determine the directional strength of evidence relative to the specific evidence object and assessment question.

strengthLevels.description: Evidence strongly indicates an unfavorable condition or significant risk.
Evidence indicates a meaningful weakness, gap, or unfavorable condition.
Evidence is inconclusive, mixed, or insufficient to establish a clear direction.
Evidence indicates a favorable condition with some remaining uncertainty.
Evidence strongly supports a favorable assessment conclusion.

evidenceContributionModel.purpose: Calculate how much influence an evidence object should have on its mapped PADF dimension assessment.

contributionRules.description: High-strength evidence with low confidence cannot receive full contribution.
Highly reliable negative evidence should reduce dimension health and trigger risk detection.
Critical evidence gaps may limit the maximum achievable dimension confidence.
Multiple independent evidence objects supporting the same conclusion may increase aggregate assessment confidence.

aggregationPrinciples: Evidence quality is more important than evidence quantity.
Duplicate evidence should not be counted as independent confirmation.
Contradictory evidence should reduce aggregate confidence.
Critical missing evidence should remain visible even when other evidence is positive.

evidenceGapIntelligence.purpose: Identify missing, weak, stale, contradictory, or insufficient evidence and prioritize evidence acquisition actions.

Evidence strength exists but reliability or validation is insufficient.

priorityLevels.description: Immediate evidence acquisition or resolution required.

Useful supporting evidence but not currently material.

historicalEvidenceEvolutionModel.purpose: Track how individual evidence objects and aggregated evidence positions evolve throughout the pipeline lifecycle.

statuses.description: Evidence exists but has not yet been evaluated.

industryAndRevenueMotionAdjustmentRules.purpose: Allow the evidence evaluation model to adapt its interpretation thresholds to specific revenue motions and industries without changing the universal scoring architecture.

Operational and cybersecurity evidence may have higher authority and validation thresholds.

evidenceEvaluationOutputModel.purpose: Define the normalized output generated after an individual evidence object is evaluated.

rules.name: EvaluateBeforeScoring

metadata.assetType: Risk Trigger & Winning Strategy Mapping Layer

riskTriggerFramework.purpose: Define the universal structure for detecting material pipeline risks from evidence conditions and assessment signals.

riskTriggerCategories.description: Risk caused by missing, incomplete, weak, or unvalidated evidence.
Risk that the customer has insufficient urgency, commitment, sponsorship, or motivation to move forward.
Risk caused by unclear, changing, inaccessible, or unfavorable decision processes.
Risk caused by weak stakeholder access, insufficient sponsorship, lack of champions, or hostile influencers.
Risk caused by incumbent advantages, competitor preference, competitive differentiation gaps, or unfavorable positioning.
Risk that the proposed solution does not sufficiently address customer requirements, business outcomes, technical requirements, or operational constraints.
Risk that the customer does not clearly recognize, quantify, validate, or prioritize the expected business value.
Risk caused by budget uncertainty, pricing pressure, procurement constraints, unfavorable commercial terms, or contracting barriers.
Risk that implementation, delivery, integration, operational readiness, or resource constraints could prevent the deal from progressing or closing.
Risk that the expected close date, buying timeline, project schedule, or customer urgency is unrealistic or deteriorating.
Risk caused by stalled progress, lack of meaningful customer interaction, insufficient evidence evolution, or repeated forecast slippage.
Risk that the opportunity is not sufficiently aligned with customer strategy, transformation priorities, investment priorities, or executive objectives.

riskTriggerTypes.description: Evidence exists but does not meet the required confidence threshold.
Reliable evidence indicates an unfavorable condition.
Material evidence sources contradict each other.
Evidence has not been sufficiently reconfirmed.
A PADF dimension falls below its configured health threshold.
The assessment conclusion for a PADF dimension lacks sufficient evidence confidence.
Evidence, dimension health, or pipeline position is deteriorating over time.
The pipeline has not demonstrated sufficient measurable progression.
A material customer, competitor, commercial, or timeline event creates elevated risk.

rootCauseHypotheses: Critical evidence acquisition activity not completed
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Acquire and validate the missing critical evidence before increasing forecast confidence.
Validate the evidence with an appropriate customer authority.

rootCauseHypotheses: Decision process has not been mapped
Seller has insufficient access to decision-makers
Procurement process is not aligned with project timeline
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Map and validate the actual decision process, stakeholders, decision criteria, and approval path.

rootCauseHypotheses: Economic buyer is protected by internal hierarchy
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Establish or improve access to the economic decision-maker or equivalent executive authority.

rootCauseHypotheses: Champion does not understand the value proposition
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Strengthen the existing champion or develop additional stakeholder advocates.
Reposition the opportunity around differentiated customer outcomes and alter the competitive basis where possible.

rootCauseHypotheses: Solution architecture misaligned with customer environment
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Validate requirements and develop a credible solution, mitigation, or alternative architecture.

rootCauseHypotheses: Economic buyer has not validated value
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Co-create and validate a customer-specific value case.

rootCauseHypotheses: Budget depends on another project or business event
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Validate funding availability, approval status, ownership, and budget release conditions.

rootCauseHypotheses: Close date based on seller expectation
Decision process not synchronized with forecast
Required milestones have not been completed
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Rebuild the close plan using customer-validated milestones and decision events.

rootCauseHypotheses: Seller lacks a clear next-step strategy
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Diagnose the cause of stagnation and create a customer-driven progression event.

rootCauseHypotheses: Solution positioned around operational features rather than strategic outcomes
universalRiskTriggers.recommendedResponseObjective: Reconnect the opportunity to a validated customer strategic priority or reconsider opportunity viability.

riskSeverityModel.purpose: Calculate the material severity of an identified pipeline risk.

severityLevels.description: Risk materially threatens the ability to win or close the pipeline without immediate intervention.
Risk has significant potential to reduce win probability.
Risk requires active management but does not currently represent a decisive threat.
Risk should be monitored and addressed as appropriate.
Limited material impact on the pipeline.

riskAggregationModel.purpose: Aggregate related risk signals without double-counting multiple symptoms of the same underlying problem.
aggregationPrinciples: Multiple triggers may represent a single root cause.
Related risks should be grouped into a risk cluster when appropriate.
Risk severity should consider both individual and cumulative impact.
Critical independent risks should remain separately visible.

winningStrategyFramework.purpose: Define the universal strategy categories that can be mapped to evidence-driven risks and pipeline weaknesses.

strategyCategories.objective: Close critical information and validation gaps.
Increase customer recognition, validation, and prioritization of business value.
Strengthen access, influence, sponsorship, and internal customer alignment.
Understand, influence, and align with the actual customer decision and approval process.
Improve competitive position through differentiation, reframing, coalition building, or competitive disruption.
Improve solution fit, technical confidence, validation, and implementation credibility.
Reduce budget, pricing, procurement, contractual, and commercial barriers.
Create a customer-validated path to decision, approval, contracting, and closure.
Align the opportunity with strategic priorities and executive outcomes.
Prevent material risk from worsening while root-cause actions are executed.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Acquire the missing critical evidence and prevent unsupported forecast confidence.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify the authoritative stakeholder who can validate the missing evidence.
Create a specific evidence acquisition action with a defined owner and deadline.
Prevent pipeline stage advancement if the evidence is configured as stage-critical.
Reassess the affected PADF dimension after evidence acquisition.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Replace assumptions or weak evidence with validated customer evidence.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify the appropriate customer authority.
Validate the evidence directly.
Document the evidence source and validation timestamp.
Replace seller inference with customer-confirmed evidence.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Build a validated decision map and align the sales process with the customer's actual buying process.
recommendedActionTemplates: Map decision criteria, decision-makers, influencers, and approval gates.
Validate the decision sequence with multiple customer stakeholders.
Identify procurement and legal dependencies.
Build a milestone-based mutual close plan.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Establish access to executive decision authority and improve strategic sponsorship.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify the economic buyer or equivalent executive authority.
Develop a stakeholder-specific executive value narrative.
Use existing sponsors to create an introduction path.
Plan an executive engagement event linked to a strategic customer outcome.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Strengthen internal customer advocacy and reduce dependence on a single weak stakeholder.
recommendedActionTemplates: Assess champion influence, motivation, and access.
Provide the champion with customer-internal value arguments.
Develop additional supporters across the buying group.
Reduce single-threaded stakeholder dependency.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Improve competitive position by changing the evaluation basis toward differentiated customer outcomes.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify the competitor's structural advantage.
Identify differentiation that matters to the customer.
Reframe evaluation criteria around business outcomes.
Strengthen customer advocates for the differentiated position.
Address competitive objections before formal evaluation or procurement gates.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Resolve material solution or technical fit concerns.
recommendedActionTemplates: Revalidate customer requirements.
Conduct technical discovery or solution workshops.
Develop proof-of-value, pilot, prototype, or technical validation where appropriate.
Define mitigation for capability gaps.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Create a customer-owned and economically credible value case.
recommendedActionTemplates: Quantify financial, operational, strategic, or risk-reduction value.
Validate assumptions with customer stakeholders.
Connect value to an executive priority.
Build a business case that can support internal approval.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Validate funding and establish a credible path through budget approval.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify the budget owner and funding source.
Validate budget availability and approval status.
Identify the remaining investment approval gates.
Strengthen the business case if budget justification is required.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Replace seller-driven close expectations with a customer-validated close path.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify all remaining decision and approval milestones.
Validate milestone dates with customer stakeholders.
Create a mutual action plan.
Reforecast the opportunity if the close path cannot support the current date.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Create a meaningful customer-driven progression event and restore pipeline momentum.
recommendedActionTemplates: Diagnose the root cause of inactivity.
Identify the next customer decision or progression event.
Create a stakeholder-specific engagement action.
Set a measurable progression milestone.
Reassess pipeline viability if momentum cannot be restored.

riskToWinningStrategyMappings.strategyObjective: Reposition the opportunity around a validated strategic priority.
recommendedActionTemplates: Identify current strategic priorities and executive objectives.
Reframe the value proposition around those priorities.
Validate strategic relevance with senior stakeholders.
Reduce investment in the pipeline if strategic alignment cannot be established.

winningStrategyPrioritizationModel.purpose: Prioritize recommended strategies and actions based on their expected impact on win probability and the urgency of the identified risk.
